title: The ALM Proxy is hardcoded as the recipient of every position, so the Relayer directs capital without ever taking custody of it
content:
In the deposit flow the encoded call is built with "the `address(proxy)` that will receive the resulting `aTokens` (i.e. ALM Proxy)" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.2.1.3.1.7.1), emitted as `proxy.doCall(address(pool), abi.encodeCall(pool.supply, (address(underlying), amount, address(proxy), 0)))`. The withdrawal flow mirrors it: the recipient argument is "the `address(proxy)` of the recipient of the withdrawn assets (i.e. ALM Proxy)" (.3.2.6.1).

The Relayer supplies only two free parameters — which `aToken` and what `amount`. The destination is not a parameter at all; it is the proxy itself, both source of the underlying and beneficiary of the receipt token.

This is what makes the Relayer role safe enough to be operational. There is no argument through which value exits the perimeter: the worst a fully compromised Relayer can do is shuffle assets between whitelisted venues and burn rate-limit capacity doing it. Theft requires compromising the proxy or the controller's function set, not the operator.

It also explains why the `Check ALM Proxy` steps exist (.3.1.2, .3.2.2) — "the operator must ensure ALM Proxy holds enough of the underlying asset" / "sufficient `aTokens`". Because the proxy is the sole balance holder, every precondition check is a check on one address, which keeps the operational runbook simple and makes monitoring a single-account problem.
description: Both the Aave supply and withdraw calls pass address(proxy) as beneficiary, meaning a compromised Relayer can move funds between whitelisted venues but cannot route them to an address of its choosing.
